sections.title: Five jobs for one word
sections.content: You know *se* in several jobs: reflexive *se* from A1 (*Ana se lava*), *se lo* from A2 Unit 25, and passive and impersonal *se* from B1 Unit 6. The same two letters also mean "each other", and they can say that something happened to you by accident. To decide which one you have, ask who does what to whom, and look at the words around *se*.

sections.title: Five kinds of se
rows: Reflexive: a person does it to themselves
Ana se lava las manos. (Ana washes her hands.)
Reciprocal: two or more people do it to each other
Los amigos se abrazan. (The friends hug each other.)
Se abren las puertas a las nueve. (The doors open at nine.)
Impersonal: nobody in particular, no noun
Aquí se vive tranquilo. (People live quietly here.)
Accidental: se + me, te, le, nos + verb
Se me cayó el vaso. (I dropped the glass; it slipped.)

items.english: They see each other every day.

items.spanish: Se ven las montañas desde aquí.
items.english: The mountains can be seen from here.

sections.content: Accidental *se* has a clue: *me*, *te*, *le*, *nos* or *les* comes right after it, and the verb agrees with the thing, not the person: *Se me cayó el vaso*, *Se me cayeron los vasos*. With a plural subject that is a person, reflexive and reciprocal can look identical (*Se saludan*). Words such as *mutuamente* ("each other") or *a sí mismos* ("themselves") remove the doubt.
